qs.q: A 65-year-old male smoker presents with progressive dysphagia initially for solids and later for liquids, accompanied by significant weight loss. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma of the mid-oesophagus. Which primary lymphatic drainage station is typically involved first?
qs.e: The oesophagus lacks a serosal layer and has an extensive longitudinal lymphatic network that drains primarily into regional mediastinal and periesophageal nodes.

qs.q: Which specific population should always be asked about freshwater exposure during history taking for haematuria due to associated squamous cell carcinoma risk?
o: Patients with chronic bacterial prostatitis infections
Patients presenting with symptomatic upper tract stones
Patients originating from Kenya and East Africa
qs.e: In Kenya and East Africa, clinicians must ask about freshwater exposure because schistosomiasis is prevalent and linked to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. It is a key regional epidemiological risk factor.

qs.q: A 53-year-old man is diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder in a Kenyan referral hospital. Aside from smoking, what is a major endemic factor contributing equally to this histology type in the region?
qs.e: In Kenya, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is as common as transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) because of schistosomiasis. Aromatic amines are classic chemical risk factors for urothelial tumours rather than the specific driver for regional SCC.

Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. In which part of the esophagus does this histologic subtype most commonly arise in this population?
o: Localized to the upper and middle thirds
qs.e: Squamous cell carcinoma in East Africa most frequently involves the upper and middle thirds of the esophagus. Adenocarcinoma, not SCC, is linked to the lower third and Barrett's changes.

qs.q: A 62‑year‑old man with biopsy‑proven esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is being staged before surgery. Why does submucosal lymphatic spread make assessment of the tumor’s longitudinal extent difficult?
qs.e: Submucosal lymphatics allow cancer cells to travel long distances, creating skip lesions that are not contiguous with the primary tumor. The other statements describe unrelated consequences of tumor spread.

qs.q: A 60-year-old patient with an upper-third squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus is scheduled for a staging workup to rule out airway invasion. Which specific investigation is mandatory alongside chest CT and EUS?
qs.e: Bronchoscopy is indicated for upper and middle third tumours to check for airway invasion. Staging laparoscopy is reserved for distal adenocarcinomas.

qs.q: A 55-year-old man undergoes an Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy for a middle-third squamous cell carcinoma. On the seventh postoperative day, before restarting oral intake, which investigation is best to safely exclude an anastomotic leak?
o: Flexible bronchoscopy to check the bronchial tree
Contrast swallow using Gastrografin or dilute barium
Computed tomography of the thorax with oral contrast
qs.e: A contrast swallow using Gastrografin or dilute barium is explicitly used after surgery to exclude an anastomotic leak before restarting oral intake. Endoscopy is avoided early on due to the risk of disrupting the fresh anastomosis.

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with an unresectable T4 squamous cell carcinoma of the upper third of the oesophagus is evaluated for palliation. Why is placement of a self-expanding metal stent strongly discouraged in this specific location?
o: Risk of airway compression and stent migration
High incidence of immediate postoperative anastomotic leak
Failure to relieve progressive dysphagia in upper lesions
Complete incompatibility with subsequent external radiotherapy
qs.e: Upper third tumours carry a specific risk of airway compression and stent migration when self-expanding metal stents are used. For this reason, alternative palliative measures like radiotherapy are often preferred for upper third SCC.

ai.title: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a malignant tumour of keratinising epithelium. In low‑resource East African settings it often arises in the cervix, bladder, skin (Marjolin ulcer) or penis, frequently linked to HPV, schistosomiasis or chronic irritation.

sections.p: SCC is a cancer of squamous epithelium that shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges on histology. Diagnosis requires a tissue sample (biopsy or excision) examined by a pathologist.
b: Biopsy shows nests of atypical squamous cells with keratinisation
Immunohistochemistry: p16 positivity suggests HPV‑related disease

sections.p: Staging follows the TNM system for each organ (e.g., cervix, bladder, skin). T describes size/invasion, N regional nodes, M distant metastases. Stage guides treatment and prognosis.
b: T1‑T4 based on depth of invasion
N0‑N3 based on nodal involvement
M0‑M1 for distant spread

sections.p: In East Africa the most common aetiologies are:
b: HPV infection (cervix, penis, vulva, vagina)
Schistosoma haematobium – chronic bladder irritation
Chronic ulcer or burn scar (Marjolin ulcer)
Tobacco smoking – lung and oral SCC
Immunosuppression (HIV) – higher HPV persistence

sections.p: Presentation depends on site but typical red‑flag symptoms include:
b: Cervical/vaginal SCC – post‑coital bleeding, foul discharge, pelvic pain
Bladder SCC – painless haematuria, irritative voiding, recurrent UTIs
Skin SCC – ulcerated, indurated lesion on scar or chronically inflamed skin
Penile SCC – ulcer or plaque on glans or shaft, often with foul smell

t.b: Confirms malignant squamous cells and grade – required for any definitive diagnosis
Identifies HPV‑driven tumour – influences prognosis and eligibility for de‑escalated therapy

t.a: Ultrasound (abdominal or pelvic) – if biopsy not available
t.b: Detects mass, hydronephrosis or bladder wall thickening; guides referral for imaging
Screens for lung metastases when CT unavailable
Elevated calcium with low PTH suggests humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy, common in SCC

sections.p: Complications arise from local invasion or systemic spread.
b: Obstructive uropathy from bladder SCC
Fistula formation (recto‑vaginal, vesico‑vaginal)
Humoral hypercalcaemia causing confusion, polyuria, renal failure
Rapid nodal or distant metastasis leading to cachexia

sections.p: Treatment combines local control, systemic therapy and symptom relief.
b: Surgery: wide local excision for skin SCC; radical hysterectomy or cystectomy for cervical/bladder disease when feasible
Radiotherapy: primary modality where surgery is not possible; especially for cervical SCC
Chemotherapy: platinum‑based doublets (cisplatin + 5‑FU) for advanced disease; avoid nephrotoxic agents if renal function impaired
Palliative care: bisphosphonates or denosumab for hypercalcaemia, analgesia, wound care for ulcerated lesions

sections.p: Long‑term surveillance prevents recurrence and detects second primaries.
b: Clinical exam every 3‑6 months for 2 years, then annually
HPV vaccination (if available) for primary prevention
Treat schistosomiasis with praziquantel to lower bladder SCC risk
Smoking cessation counseling

sections.p: Conditions that mimic SCC clinically or histologically:
b: Verrucous carcinoma – well‑differentiated, less aggressive variant
Basal cell carcinoma – pearly papule, rare in mucosal sites
Chronic ulcer or granuloma – may look similar before biopsy
Normal serum calcium does not exclude early humoral hypercalcaemia; repeat if symptoms develop
HPV‑negative SCC can still be aggressive – do not rely solely on p16
Ultrasound may miss small nodal metastases; clinical exam remains essential

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe haematuria with clot retention
Rapidly enlarging ulcerated skin lesion with foul discharge
New onset confusion, polyuria and serum calcium >12 mg/dL

faq.q: Why is HPV testing important in SCC?
faq.a: HPV positivity predicts better response to radiotherapy and may allow treatment de‑escalation.

faq.q: Can SCC cause high calcium without bone metastasis?
faq.a: Yes, SCC often secretes PTH‑related peptide, causing humoral hypercalcaemia.

faq.q: What is the role of surgery in bladder SCC in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Radical cystectomy offers the best chance of cure but may be limited; partial cystectomy or palliative radiotherapy are alternatives.

exam: A 55‑year‑old woman from a rural clinic presents with post‑coital bleeding; what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Obtain a cervical biopsy to confirm SCC; visual inspection alone cannot rule out malignancy.
How does chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection lead to bladder SCC? — Repeated irritation causes squamous metaplasia, which can undergo malignant transformation.

A patient with known lung SCC develops confusion and a calcium of 13 mg/dL; what does this indicate and how should you manage it? — Suggests humoral hypercalcaemia; give IV fluids, bisphosphonate, and test PTHrP.

What are the key histological features that differentiate SCC from verrucous carcinoma? — SCC shows keratin pearls and atypia; verrucous carcinoma is well‑differentiated with minimal atypia and pushing borders.
In a setting without CT, how would you stage a cervical SCC? — Use clinical exam for tumour size, palpate parametrial involvement, assess nodal status, and perform chest X‑ray for distant spread.
Why is cisplatin preferred over methotrexate in advanced SCC when renal function is borderline? — Cisplatin has higher response rates; methotrexate is more nephrotoxic and less effective in SCC.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a penile ulcer? — Rapidly enlarging ulcer with foul smell or bleeding, suggesting invasive SCC.
Explain why smoking cessation is part of SCC management even after tumour removal. — Ongoing tobacco exposure increases risk of second primary tumours and impairs wound healing.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam reveal the site, risk factors and local invasion of SCC and help differentiate it from mimics.
b: Duration and evolution of the lesion or symptom (weeks vs months).
Site‑specific symptoms: bleeding, dysphagia, urinary changes, pain, ulceration, foul discharge.
Risk‑factor enquiry: tobacco, alcohol, HPV exposure, freshwater contact, chronic ulcer or scar, schistosomiasis, HIV status, immunosuppression, occupational irritants.
Systemic red‑flags: weight loss, night sweats, bone pain, hypercalcaemia symptoms.
Previous lesions or treatments, family cancer history, vaccination status (HPV).

t.b: Identify size, colour, ulceration, induration, or exophytic growth; a raised, keratinised nodule suggests SCC, but cannot determine depth of invasion.
Firm, fixed tissue indicates deeper invasion or desmoplastic reaction; mobility suggests superficial disease; cannot measure exact depth.
Palpate for size >1 cm, fixation, matting; positive nodes raise N stage but cannot differentiate reactive from metastatic without imaging.

t.a: Digital rectal or pelvic exam (when indicated)
t.b: Detect fixation, nodularity, or ulceration of rectum, vagina or prostate; a fixed mass suggests T3/T4 disease, but cannot stage exact depth.
Observe stridor, voice change, cough; bedside cannot quantify airway narrowing – requires endoscopy.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select investigations that answer the key clinical questions of histology, extent, nodal status and distant spread; include alternatives for low‑resource settings.
b: Biopsy (incisional or excisional) – confirms SCC; keratin pearls and intercellular bridges are diagnostic.
p16 immunohistochemistry – surrogate for high‑risk HPV; positivity supports HPV‑related SCC but is not a prognostic marker alone.
Ultrasound of regional nodes – assesses size, shape, hilum; loss of hilum or >1 cm suggests metastatic involvement.
Chest X‑ray (where CT unavailable) – screens for lung metastases or primary lung SCC; new nodules >1 cm are suspicious.
Abdominal ultrasound – evaluates bladder wall thickening, hydronephrosis; irregular wall >5 mm raises suspicion for muscle invasion.
Basic labs (CBC, calcium, renal function) – hypercalcaemia (>12 mg/dL) suggests humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy; anemia may indicate chronic blood loss.

t.b: Answers: Is the lesion SCC? Look for keratin pearls, intercellular bridges; presence of dysplasia or carcinoma in situ indicates precursor lesion.
Answers: Is HPV likely involved? Strong nuclear and cytoplasmic staining supports HPV‑related SCC; negative does not exclude SCC.
Answers: Are nodes involved? Nodes >1 cm, round, loss of fatty hilum = metastatic; if unavailable, rely on clinical palpation.
Answers: Is there pulmonary metastasis? New opacities or nodules >1 cm suggest spread; if equivocal, arrange referral for CT when possible.
Answers: Is there muscle invasion? Irregular wall >5 mm or loss of smooth contour suggests T2+; if unavailable, cystoscopy is the next step.
Answers: Is humoral hypercalcaemia present? Calcium ≥12 mg/dL indicates paraneoplastic syndrome; triggers work‑up for bone mets and palliative measures.

sections.p: Staging follows organ‑specific TNM systems; severity combines stage with performance status and comorbidities.
b: Confirm diagnosis histologically with SCC features.
Assign T stage according to organ: e.g., skin T1 ≤2 cm, T2 >2 cm ≤5 cm, T3 >5 cm or deep invasion; bladder T1 lamina propria, T2 muscle, T3 perivesical fat.
Assign N stage organ‑specifically: N0 no regional nodes, N1 single ipsilateral node ≤3 cm, N2 multiple or >3 cm, N3 contralateral or supraclavicular nodes.
Assign M stage: M0 no distant disease, M1 distant metastasis (lung, bone, liver).
Combine TNM into stage group (I‑IV) per AJCC 8th edition for the specific site.
Assess performance status (ECOG 0‑2 for curative intent).
Note HIV positivity or severe malnutrition as factors that may up‑stage functional status.

sections.p: Several lesions mimic SCC clinically or histologically; careful correlation of history, exam and targeted tests separates them.
b: Verrucous carcinoma – exophytic, warty lesion; histology shows minimal atypia, broad pushing borders, no keratin pearls; p16 usually negative.
Basal cell carcinoma – ulcerated nodule with pearly border; histology shows peripheral palisading, mucinous stroma; lacks intercellular bridges.
Marjolin ulcer (squamous carcinoma arising in chronic scar) – history of burn or ulcer; same histology as SCC but preceded by long‑standing scar.
Keratoacanthoma – rapid‑growing dome‑shaped nodule with central keratin plug; histology shows well‑circumscribed crater; may regress spontaneously.

t.b: History of chronic scar or burn points to Marjolin ulcer; absence suggests de novo SCC.
Broad pushing margins without infiltrative nests favour verrucous carcinoma; infiltrative nests with keratin pearls confirm SCC.
Positive in HPV‑related SCC; usually negative in basal cell carcinoma and verrucous carcinoma.

sections.p: A pragmatic ladder for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) that can be applied across organ sites in low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Confirm diagnosis with adequate biopsy; send for H&E and p16 if HPV‑related disease is suspected.
2. Stage clinically using organ‑specific TNM (size, depth, nodal palpation, distant symptoms) when imaging is unavailable.
3. Multidisciplinary decision: surgery for resectable disease, definitive radiotherapy ± concurrent cisplatin for non‑resectable or organ‑preserving intent.
5. Post‑treatment surveillance: clinical exam every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months; imaging only if new symptoms.
6. Escalate to palliative radiotherapy, systemic immunotherapy (PD‑1 inhibitor) or best‑supportive care when progression occurs or performance status declines.
7. Refer to tertiary centre for complex reconstruction, clinical trials, or management of severe complications.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key toxicities of agents used in SCC and practical mitigation strategies.
b: Cisplatin – nephrotoxicity: ensure adequate hydration, avoid concurrent nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs); monitor creatinine before each cycle.
Cisplatin – ototoxicity: ask about tinnitus, perform audiometry if available; consider dose reduction or switch to carboplatin if hearing loss emerges.
Cisplatin – nausea/vomiting: give a 5‑HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone pre‑medication; use metoclopramide if breakthrough.
Cisplatin – peripheral neuropathy: assess for tingling; if grade 2+, pause treatment and consider substitution.
PD‑1 inhibitors – immune‑related pneumonitis: obtain chest X‑ray if new dyspnoea; start steroids promptly.
PD‑1 inhibitors – colitis: monitor stool frequency; treat grade 2+ with steroids and hold immunotherapy.
Radiotherapy – skin ulceration: keep area clean, use non‑adhesive dressings; refer for wound care if necrosis develops.
Radiotherapy – oesophageal stricture: assess dysphagia; dilatation endoscopically if severe.

sections.p: Complications that signal need for urgent referral or change in treatment plan.
b: Rapidly enlarging ulcer or foul discharge → suspect infection or malignant fistula; obtain culture and refer for surgical assessment.
New onset hoarseness or stridor in head‑neck SCC → possible airway invasion; arrange urgent airway imaging and ENT review.
Progressive dysphagia with weight loss despite stent → consider tumour overgrowth; refer for re‑stenting or palliative radiotherapy.
Unexplained fever, night sweats, and lymphadenopathy → rule out TB co‑infection; send sputum for GeneXpert and refer to TB programme.
Severe mucositis (grade 3) impairing oral intake → start opioid analgesia, nutritional support, and pause chemoradiation until healing.

sections.p: How common comorbidities and contextual issues modify presentation, investigations and therapy.
b: HIV infection – higher HPV persistence; CD4 <200 cells/µL may reduce chemotherapy tolerance; ensure ART adherence and consider prophylactic PCP.
Tuberculosis – chronic cough may mask oesophageal SCC; perform sputum GeneXpert when respiratory symptoms present.
Malnutrition – low albumin (<30 g/L) predicts poor wound healing; provide high‑protein oral supplements before surgery.
Pregnancy – avoid radiotherapy and cisplatin in first trimester; consider surgery if feasible, otherwise defer definitive therapy until postpartum.
Diabetes – hyperglycaemia worsens wound infection risk; optimise glucose before any operative procedure.
Herbal remedies (e.g., St. John’s wort) – can induce CYP enzymes, lowering cisplatin efficacy; counsel patients to stop them.
Alcohol abuse – increases liver toxicity and interferes with wound healing; screen and offer brief intervention.
Renal failure – cisplatin contraindicated when eGFR <30 mL/min; use carboplatin or radiotherapy alone.
Advanced age (>75 years) – higher risk of treatment‑related toxicity; favour hypofractionated radiotherapy and careful renal monitoring.

sections.p: Tailored considerations for vulnerable populations in low‑resource environments.
b: Children – SCC rare; when present (e.g., oral), prioritize surgery with clear margins; avoid radiotherapy when possible due to growth‑plate damage.
Pregnancy – stage‑appropriate surgery in second trimester; postpone systemic therapy until after delivery; use shielding if imaging required.
People with HIV – integrate oncology and HIV services; continue ART; monitor for drug‑drug interactions (e.g., protease inhibitors increasing cisplatin nephrotoxicity).
Low‑resource settings – use clinical staging (palpable nodes, ulcer size) when CT unavailable; employ hypofractionated radiotherapy schedules; rely on generic cisplatin rather than newer agents.

sections.p: Sample questions to test mastery of the above material.
b: 1. Which bedside sign helps differentiate a malignant ulcer from a simple chronic wound? Explain its technique and limitation.
2. A patient with cervical SCC has a serum calcium of 13 mg/dL. What does this indicate and how should you manage it?
3. How would you stage a bladder SCC clinically when ultrasound is the only imaging modality?
4. List three drug–drug interactions that require stopping a herbal remedy before starting cisplatin.
5. In a HIV‑positive man with oesophageal SCC, what modification to concurrent chemoradiation is recommended?
6. Describe the management steps when a patient develops grade 3 mucositis during chemoradiation.
7. What is the preferred systemic agent for palliation of metastatic SCC when renal function is borderline?
8. How does chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection lead to bladder SCC at the molecular level?
9. A pregnant woman in her second trimester presents with a 3 cm oral SCC. Outline the definitive treatment plan.
10. When is it acceptable to use hypofractionated radiotherapy for SCC in a low‑resource centre, and what schedule is commonly used?

Complications: local invasion causing obstruction (bladder SCC), fistula formation, humoral hypercalcaemia, rapid nodal/distant metastasis.

vivas.q: A 55‑year‑old woman presents with post‑coital bleeding. What is the next step?
vivas.a: Perform a speculum examination and obtain a cervical biopsy to confirm SCC.

vivas.q: How does chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection lead to bladder SCC?
vivas.a: Repeated bladder irritation and chronic inflammation cause squamous metaplasia, dysplasia and eventually malignant transformation.

vivas.q: A patient with lung SCC develops confusion and a calcium of 13 mg/dL. What does this indicate?
vivas.a: Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy, often due to PTHrP secretion, requiring calcium‑lowering therapy and treating the tumour.

vivas.q: What histological feature differentiates SCC from verrucous carcinoma?
vivas.a: Verrucous carcinoma shows broad pushing borders and minimal atypia, whereas SCC has keratin pearls, intercellular bridges and cytologic atypia.

vivas.q: In a setting without CT, how would you stage a cervical SCC?
vivas.a: Use clinical staging: digital rectal exam, speculum exam, and pelvic ultrasound if available; rely on tumour size and nodal assessment by palpation.

vivas.q: What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a penile ulcer?
vivas.a: Foul‑smelling, rapidly enlarging ulcer with induration and possible lymphadenopathy.

vivas.q: Explain why smoking cessation is part of SCC management even after tumour removal.
vivas.a: It reduces recurrence risk, prevents second primary tumours, and improves overall survival.

vivas.q: A 65‑year‑old male smoker presents with progressive dysphagia. Biopsy confirms mid‑oesophageal SCC. Which treatment is most appropriate?
vivas.a: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by oesophagectomy if fit; otherwise definitive chemoradiotherapy.

vivas.q: Which specific population should always be asked about freshwater exposure during history taking for haematuria due to associated SCC risk?
vivas.a: People living around Lake Victoria or other endemic schistosomiasis areas.

vivas.q: A 53‑year‑old man is diagnosed with bladder SCC in Kenya. Aside from smoking, what is a major endemic factor contributing equally to this histology type?
A 58‑year‑old Kenyan man presents with progressive dysphagia. Biopsy shows SCC. In which stage is the tumour likely to be?
vivas.a: T3 or T4, as mid‑oesophageal SCC often presents late with invasion beyond muscularis.

vivas.q: Why does submucosal lymphatic spread make assessment of the tumour’s longitudinal extent difficult?
vivas.a: Submucosal nodes are not palpable and imaging may miss them, leading to under‑staging of tumour length.

vivas.q: Which investigation is mandatory alongside chest CT and EUS to rule out airway invasion in upper‑third oesophageal SCC?
vivas.a: Bronchoscopy with biopsy or brush cytology.

vivas.q: Which investigation is best to safely exclude an anastomotic leak before restarting oral intake after Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy?
vivas.a: Contrast swallow study (barium swallow) to detect leak.

vivas.q: Detail the risk factors and morphological variants of penile SCC.
vivas.a: Risk factors: HPV infection, phimosis, chronic inflammation, smoking, HIV. Variants: keratinising, basaloid, warty, verrucous.

mcqs.q: A 60‑year‑old man with upper‑third oesophageal SCC is scheduled for staging. Which investigation is mandatory to assess airway invasion?
A patient with bladder SCC has a calcium of 13 mg/dL. Which is the most likely cause?
mcqs.e: SCC often secretes PTHrP causing humoral hypercalcaemia.

mcqs.q: Which IHC marker indicates HPV‑related cervical SCC?
mcqs.e: p16 overexpression is a surrogate for high‑risk HPV infection.

mcqs.q: A 55‑year‑old woman with post‑coital bleeding should first undergo which examination?
Which factor is NOT a risk for cutaneous SCC?
mcqs.e: HPV is not a major risk for skin SCC.

mcqs.q: Cisplatin is preferred over methotrexate in advanced SCC because:
mcqs.e: Cisplatin has proven efficacy in SCC.

mcqs.q: Which sign is most specific for bladder SCC?
mcqs.e: Painless haematuria is classic for bladder SCC.

mcqs.q: Which imaging modality is best to assess nodal involvement in cervical SCC when CT is unavailable?
mcqs.e: Pelvic ultrasound can detect enlarged nodes when CT is not available.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Penile squamous cell carcinoma, keratinising type.

cases.v: A 70‑year‑old woman from rural Kenya reports painless haematuria for 3 months. She is a chronic smoker and lives near Lake Victoria. Cystoscopy shows a papillary tumour on the bladder wall.

qs.q: What is the most likely histology?
qs.a: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

qs.q: Which endemic infection should be investigated?
What is the first step in staging?
qs.a: Clinical staging with digital rectal exam, cystoscopy findings and ultrasound for nodal assessment.

mistakes: Assuming all SCCs use the same TNM criteria; staging is organ‑specific.
Confusing p16 positivity as a prognostic marker; it indicates HPV infection, not prognosis.
Over‑relying on CT for cervical SCC staging when clinical exam is adequate.
Mistaking methotrexate for a first‑line agent in SCC; cisplatin is standard.
Ignoring the possibility of humoral hypercalcaemia in SCC presenting with confusion.
Failing to recognise that smoking cessation is essential even after tumour removal.
Misidentifying verrucous carcinoma as SCC based solely on keratin pearls.
Assuming bladder SCC always presents with painful haematuria; it is usually painless.
exam: A 55‑year‑old woman presents with post‑coital bleeding. What is the next step? — Perform a speculum examination and obtain a cervical biopsy to confirm SCC.

How does chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection lead to bladder SCC? — Repeated bladder irritation and chronic inflammation cause squamous metaplasia, dysplasia and eventually malignant transformation.

A patient with lung SCC develops confusion and a calcium of 13 mg/dL. What does this indicate? — Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy, often due to PTHrP secretion, requiring calcium‑lowering therapy and treating the tumour.

What histological feature differentiates SCC from verrucous carcinoma? — Verrucous carcinoma shows broad pushing borders and minimal atypia, whereas SCC has keratin pearls, intercellular bridges and cytologic atypia.

In a setting without CT, how would you stage a cervical SCC? — Use clinical staging: digital rectal exam, speculum exam, and pelvic ultrasound if available; rely on tumour size and nodal assessment by palpation.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a penile ulcer? — Foul‑smelling, rapidly enlarging ulcer with induration and possible lymphadenopathy.
Explain why smoking cessation is part of SCC management even after tumour removal. — It reduces recurrence risk, prevents second primary tumours, and improves overall survival.

A 65‑year‑old male smoker presents with progressive dysphagia. Biopsy confirms mid‑oesophageal SCC. Which treatment is most appropriate? — Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by oesophagectomy if fit; otherwise definitive chemoradiotherapy.

Which specific population should always be asked about freshwater exposure during history taking for haematuria due to associated SCC risk? — People living around Lake Victoria or other endemic schistosomiasis areas.
A 53‑year‑old man is diagnosed with bladder SCC in Kenya. Aside from smoking, what is a major endemic factor contributing equally to this histology type? — Schistosoma haematobium infection.

A 58‑year‑old Kenyan man presents with progressive dysphagia. Biopsy shows SCC. In which stage is the tumour likely to be? — T3 or T4, as mid‑oesophageal SCC often presents late with invasion beyond muscularis.

Why does submucosal lymphatic spread make assessment of the tumour’s longitudinal extent difficult? — Submucosal nodes are not palpable and imaging may miss them, leading to under‑staging of tumour length.
Which investigation is mandatory alongside chest CT and EUS to rule out airway invasion in upper‑third oesophageal SCC? — Bronchoscopy with biopsy or brush cytology.
Which investigation is best to safely exclude an anastomotic leak before restarting oral intake after Ivor Lewis oesophagectomy? — Contrast swallow study (barium swallow) to detect leak.
